code.title: Dividing under a prime modulus: multiply by the modular inverse
code.python:
P = 1_000_000_007


# Fast power: square the base and halve the exponent, O(log e)
def power(b, e):
    r = 1
    b %= P
    while e > 0:
        if e & 1:
            r = r * b % P
        b = b * b % P
        e >>= 1
    return r


a, b = 84, 12
# Fermat: b^(P-2) is the inverse of b because P is prime
inv = power(b, P - 2)
# "a divided by b" becomes "a times the inverse of b"
q = a % P * inv % P
print("a=" + str(a) + " b=" + str(b) + " p=" + str(P))
print("inverse of b = " + str(inv))
print("a/b mod p = " + str(q))
print("check b*inverse mod p = " + str(b * inv % P))
# Time O(log p), space O(1)

followUps:
Fermat's shortcut stops working, because it needs a prime modulus and 109 = 29·59 is not prime. An inverse of b now exists only when gcd(b, 109) = 1, that is, when b is not divisible by 2 or 5. In that case find it with Extended Euclid in O(log m), or as bφ(m)−1 with φ(109) = 4·108.

Small example mod 10: the inverse of 3 is 7 (3·7 = 21, remainder 1), but 4 has no inverse because 4·x always ends in an even digit. When b shares a factor with the modulus you must avoid dividing at all: build the answer with additions only (Pascal's triangle), or keep the powers of 2 and 5 in separate counters and multiply them back at the end.

Use the rule inv[i] = (p − p/i) · inv[p % i] % p with inv[1] = 1; each inverse is built from a smaller one, so the whole table costs O(N) time and O(N) space instead of N fast powers.

Why it works: write p = q·i + r with q = p/i, r = p % i. Mod p this says q·i ≡ −r, so i−1 ≡ −q · r−1, and r < i is already in the table.

inv[1] = 1;
for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++)
    inv[i] = (p - p / i) * inv[p % i] % p;

Check with p = 7: inv[2] = (7 − 3)·inv[1] = 4 and 2·4 = 8 ≡ 1; inv[3] = (7 − 2)·inv[1] = 5 and 3·5 = 15 ≡ 1. It needs p prime and n < p.

code.title: Extended Euclid: gcd plus the coefficients x and y
code.python:
# Returns (g, x, y) with a*x + b*y = g = gcd(a, b)
def ext(a, b):
    # Base case: gcd(a, 0) = a = a*1 + 0*0
    if b == 0:
        return a, 1, 0
    # Solve the smaller problem (b, a mod b) first
    g, x1, y1 = ext(b, a % b)
    # Update rule: x = y1, y = x1 - (a/b)*y1
    return g, y1, x1 - (a // b) * y1


a, b = 240, 46
g, x, y = ext(a, b)
print("a=" + str(a) + " b=" + str(b))
print("gcd=" + str(g) + " x=" + str(x) + " y=" + str(y))
print("check a*x + b*y = " + str(a * x + b * y))
# Time O(log min(a, b)), space O(log min(a, b)) for the recursion

followUps:
Keep two pairs of coefficients, one for the current a and one for the current b, and update them with the same quotient that Euclid's loop uses.

long x0 = 1, y0 = 0, x1 = 0, y1 = 1, q, t;
while (b != 0) {
  q = a / b;  t = a - q * b;  a = b;  b = t;
  t = x0 - q * x1;  x0 = x1;  x1 = t;
  t = y0 - q * y1;  y0 = y1;  y1 = t;
}   // gcd = a, x = x0, y = y0

The loop keeps two facts true: (original a)·x0 + (original b)·y0 = current a, and the same with x1, y1 for current b. For a = 240, b = 46 it ends with gcd 2, x = −9, y = 47, and 240·(−9) + 46·47 = 2. Time O(log min(a, b)), space O(1), with no recursion stack.

There are solutions only when g = gcd(a, b) divides c; then there are infinitely many, all reached from one of them by a fixed step.

  1. Run Extended Euclid to get a·x + b·y = g.
  2. Scale: x0 = x·(c/g), y0 = y·(c/g) is one solution.
  3. All solutions: x = x0 + k·(b/g), y = y0 − k·(a/g) for any integer k. The extra parts cancel: a·k·b/g − b·k·a/g = 0.

Example 6x + 4y = 10: g = 2 and 6·1 + 4·(−1) = 2. Scale by 5 to get (5, −5). General form x = 5 + 2k, y = −5 − 3k; k = −2 gives (1, 1), and 6 + 4 = 10. For 6x + 4y = 7 there is nothing, since 2 does not divide 7. Cost O(log min(a, b)).

code.title: Fermat's inverse gives a silent wrong answer for a composite modulus
code.python:
def power(b, e, m):
    r = 1 % m
    b %= m
    while e > 0:
        if e & 1:
            r = r * b % m
        b = b * b % m
        e >>= 1
    return r


# Extended Euclid: returns (g, x, y) with a*x + b*y = g
def ext(a, b):
    if b == 0:
        return a, 1, 0
    g, x1, y1 = ext(b, a % b)
    return g, y1, x1 - (a // b) * y1


a, m = 5, 12  # 12 is NOT prime
# Fermat's formula a^(m-2): only valid when m is prime
fermat = power(a, m - 2, m)
# Extended Euclid works for any m, as long as gcd(a, m) = 1
g, x, y = ext(a, m)
euclid = (x % m + m) % m  # make it non-negative
print("a=" + str(a) + " m=" + str(m))
print("Fermat gives " + str(fermat) + ", a*result mod m = " + str(a * fermat % m))
print("Euclid gives " + str(euclid) + ", a*result mod m = " + str(a * euclid % m))
# No crash: the Fermat result is simply wrong (the product is not 1)
# Time O(log m) for both, space O(log m) for the recursion

followUps:
Test the one property that defines an inverse: for every result, a · inv % m must equal 1, and you check that directly rather than comparing with another formula.

  • Composite moduli: m = 12, 109, 232. With m = 12, a = 5 the correct answer is 5; a Fermat-based function returns 1 and the test fails at once.
  • No inverse: a = 0, a = m, a = 4 with m = 12. Expect an error or a clear "none" value, never a number.
  • Brute force: for every m up to 200 and every a < m, compare with a loop that tries all candidates.
  • Edges: m = 1, a larger than m, negative a, and values near 1018 to catch overflow in the multiplication.

RSA does: the private exponent is d = e−1 mod φ(n), where φ(n) = (p − 1)(q − 1) is an even number and so never prime. Fermat's formula is useless there, so key generation uses Extended Euclid, after checking gcd(e, φ(n)) = 1.

Tiny example: p = 3, q = 11 gives n = 33 and φ(n) = 2·10 = 20. Pick e = 3. Extended Euclid gives d = 7, because 3·7 = 21 leaves remainder 1 when divided by 20. Encrypting 2 gives 23 = 8, and decrypting gives 87 mod 33 = 2 again. The cost is O(log φ(n)) steps on big integers.

code.title: Euler's totient: one number by trial division, all numbers by a sieve

followUps:
It fails when a and n share a factor, because Euler's theorem only promises aφ(n) ≡ 1 for gcd(a, n) = 1.

Example: n = 4, φ(4) = 2, a = 2, b = 2. The true value is 22 mod 4 = 0, but the shortcut gives 22 mod 2 = 20 = 1. Wrong.

The safe rule works for every a: if b ≥ φ(n), use a(b mod φ(n)) + φ(n); if b is smaller, use b itself. Here that gives 20+2 = 4 ≡ 0, which is correct. This is the rule to use for power towers such as abc mod n, where the exponent is too large to store. Each level costs O(√n) for φ plus O(log) for the power.

The number of ordered pairs (i, j) with 1 ≤ i, j ≤ N and gcd(i, j) = 1 is 2·(φ(1) + φ(2) + … + φ(N)) − 1.

Reason: for a fixed j, exactly φ(j) values i ≤ j are coprime with j, so the sum counts pairs with i ≤ j. Doubling adds the mirrored pairs, and (1, 1), the only coprime pair with i = j, was counted twice, so subtract 1.

for (i = 0; i <= N; i++) phi[i] = i;
for (p = 2; p <= N; p++) if (phi[p] == p)
    for (j = p; j <= N; j += p) phi[j] -= phi[j] / p;
long sum = 0;
for (i = 1; i <= N; i++) sum += phi[i];
long answer = 2 * sum - 1;

N = 3: 2·(1 + 1 + 2) − 1 = 7, the pairs (1,1), (1,2), (2,1), (1,3), (3,1), (2,3), (3,2). Time O(N log log N), space O(N).

code.title: CRT with non-coprime moduli: merge two congruences or report no solution
code.python:
# Extended Euclid: (g, x, y) with a*x + b*y = g
def ext(a, b):
    if b == 0:
        return a, 1, 0
    g, x1, y1 = ext(b, a % b)
    return g, y1, x1 - (a // b) * y1


# Merge x = a1 (mod m1) and x = a2 (mod m2); returns (x, lcm) or None
def merge(a1, m1, a2, m2):
    g, x, y = ext(m1, m2)
    # No solution unless g divides the difference of the remainders
    if (a2 - a1) % g != 0:
        return None
    mod = m2 // g
    # x is the inverse of m1/g modulo m2/g
    k = ((a2 - a1) // g % mod) * (x % mod) % mod
    k = (k + mod) % mod
    lcm = m1 // g * m2
    # answer = a1 + m1*k, unique modulo lcm(m1, m2)
    return (a1 + m1 * k) % lcm, lcm


def show(a1, m1, a2, m2):
    r = merge(a1, m1, a2, m2)
    head = "x = " + str(a1) + " (mod " + str(m1) + "), x = " + str(a2) + " (mod " + str(m2) + ") -> "
    if r is None:
        print(head + "no solution")
    else:
        print(head + "x = " + str(r[0]) + " (mod " + str(r[1]) + ")")


show(2, 6, 8, 10)   # gcd 2 divides 8-2
show(1, 6, 4, 10)   # gcd 2 does not divide 4-1
show(8, 30, 3, 7)   # fold in a third congruence
# Time O(log min(m1, m2)) per merge, space O(log) for the recursion

followUps:
You cannot simply reduce x mod 109+7 while merging, because the next merge needs the exact x modulo the next modulus. Use Garner's algorithm, which never builds the huge number.

Write the answer in mixed radix: x = c0 + c1·m0 + c2·m0·m1 + …. Each digit c_i is smaller than m_i and is found using arithmetic mod m_i only. Then evaluate the same sum mod 109+7.

Example x ≡ 2 (mod 3), x ≡ 3 (mod 5): c0 = 2; c1 = (3 − 2)·3−1 mod 5 = 1·2 = 2; x = 2 + 2·3 = 8. Garner needs pairwise coprime moduli, so first split each modulus into prime powers, check that they agree, and keep the highest power of each prime. Time O(k²) for k moduli. In Python or Java you can also keep x as a big integer and reduce once at the end.

RSA uses CRT to make decryption about four times faster: instead of one big power modulo n = p·q, it does two half-size powers modulo p and modulo q and glues the results together.

Compute m_p = cd mod (p−1) mod p and m_q = cd mod (q−1) mod q, then find the one m below n with those two remainders. Numbers half as long make each multiplication about 4 times cheaper and the exponent half as long, so each power is about 8 times cheaper, and there are two of them.

Example p = 3, q = 11, d = 7, c = 2: directly 27 = 128 mod 33 = 29. With CRT: m_p = 27 mod 2 mod 3 = 2, m_q = 27 mod 11 = 7, and the number below 33 that is 2 mod 3 and 7 mod 11 is 29.

code.title: Fibonacci for n = 10^18 with 2x2 matrix exponentiation
code.python:
P = 1_000_000_007


# Multiply two 2x2 matrices, reducing mod P after every product
def mul(a, b):
    c = [[0, 0], [0, 0]]
    for i in range(2):
        for j in range(2):
            c[i][j] = (a[i][0] * b[0][j] % P + a[i][1] * b[1][j] % P) % P
    return c


def fib(n):
    result = [[1, 0], [0, 1]]   # identity matrix
    base = [[1, 1], [1, 0]]     # the step matrix T
    # Binary exponentiation: one squaring per bit of n
    while n > 0:
        if n & 1:
            result = mul(result, base)
        base = mul(base, base)
        n >>= 1
    # T^n = [[F(n+1), F(n)], [F(n), F(n-1)]]
    return result[0][1]


big = 10 ** 18
print("F(10) = " + str(fib(10)))
print("F(" + str(big) + ") mod " + str(P) + " = " + str(fib(big)))
# Time O(8 log n) = about 60 squarings, space O(1)

followUps:
Add a constant 1 to the state so the "+5" becomes part of the matrix. The state is [f(n), f(n−1), 1] and one step is:

| f(n)   |   | 3 2 5 |   | f(n-1) |
| f(n-1) | = | 1 0 0 | * | f(n-2) |
|   1    |   | 0 0 1 |   |   1    |

Row 1 is the recurrence, row 2 copies the old value down, row 3 keeps the 1 alive. Raise the 3×3 matrix to the power n − 1 and multiply by [f(1), f(0), 1].

Check with f(0) = 0, f(1) = 1: the first row gives 3·1 + 2·0 + 5·1 = 8, and by hand f(2) = 3 + 0 + 5 = 8. Then f(3) = 3·8 + 2·1 + 5 = 31. Time O(3³ · log n) = about 27 multiplications per squaring, space O(1).

Raise the adjacency matrix A to the power k: the entry (Ak)[u][v] is exactly the number of walks with k edges from u to v.

Reason: (A·A)[u][v] = sum over w of A[u][w]·A[w][v], which counts every middle vertex w that links u to v, so A² counts 2-step walks. Each further multiplication adds one more edge.

Example, a triangle 0-1-2: A² has 2 on the diagonal (go to either neighbour and come back) and 1 elsewhere (one way through the third vertex). Total closed walks of length k is the sum of the diagonal.

Time O(V³ log k) with binary exponentiation, space O(V²). Counts grow fast, so reduce mod p after every multiplication. "At most k edges" is handled by adding a self-loop on a helper vertex.

code.title: Small n: a plain loop beats matrix power (Tribonacci, work counted)
code.python:
mat_muls = 0


def mul(a, b):
    global mat_muls
    mat_muls += 1  # each call costs k^3 = 27 scalar multiplications
    c = [[0] * 3 for _ in range(3)]
    for i in range(3):
        for j in range(3):
            for k in range(3):
                c[i][j] += a[i][k] * b[k][j]
    return c


n = 30  # T(0)=0, T(1)=0, T(2)=1, T(n)=T(n-1)+T(n-2)+T(n-3)
# Way 1: simple loop, one cheap step per term
a, b, c = 0, 0, 1
steps = 0
for i in range(3, n + 1):
    a, b, c = b, c, a + b + c
    steps += 1
# Way 2: raise the 3x3 step matrix to the power n-2
result = [[1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1]]
base = [[1, 1, 1], [1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0]]
e = n - 2
while e > 0:
    if e & 1:
        result = mul(result, base)
    e >>= 1
    if e > 0:
        base = mul(base, base)
print("n=" + str(n) + " state size k=3")
print("loop:   T(n)=" + str(c) + " using " + str(steps) + " loop steps")
print("matrix: T(n)=" + str(result[0][0]) + " using " + str(mat_muls)
      + " matrix products = " + str(mat_muls * 27) + " scalar multiplications")
# Loop O(n*k) time; matrix O(k^3 log n) time: it only wins for huge n

followUps:
Kitamasa writes the far term as a fixed mix of the first k terms, f(n) = c0·f(0) + … + c(k−1)·f(k−1), and finds the k coefficients by doubling n, so it handles k numbers instead of a k×k matrix.

The coefficients of n are the polynomial xn reduced modulo the characteristic polynomial. To go from n to 2n, multiply the coefficient polynomial by itself (O(k²)), then push every power ≥ k back down with the recurrence (O(k²)). Repeat like binary exponentiation: O(k² log n) time, O(k) space.

Fibonacci example: the rule is x² = x + 1. Then x4 = (x + 1)² = x² + 2x + 1 = 3x + 2, so F(4) = 3·F(1) + 2·F(0) = 3. For k = 500 and n = 1018 this is about 3·107 steps, where the matrix needs about 1010.

It computes shortest paths that use an exact number of edges: replace "multiply" by "add" and "add" by "take the minimum", so C[i][j] = min over k of (A[i][k] + B[k][j]).

If A holds edge weights (infinity where there is no edge), then A² under this product is the cheapest 2-edge path between every pair, and Ak is the cheapest path with exactly k edges. The product is associative, so binary exponentiation works: O(V³ log k) time, O(V²) space.

Example: edges 0→1 with cost 2, 1→2 with cost 3, 0→2 with cost 9. A²[0][2] = 2 + 3 = 5, the best 2-edge route. Typical uses: "cheapest route with exactly k flights" for huge k, and any DP whose step is "min of previous value plus a cost" repeated many times. Put 0 on the diagonal to get "at most k edges".

code.title: Inclusion-exclusion over bitmasks: numbers up to N divisible by 2, 3 or 5
code.python:
from math import gcd

N = 100
d = [2, 3, 5]
k = len(d)
total = 0
# Every non-empty subset of the divisors is one bitmask
for mask in range(1, 1 << k):
    lcm = 1
    bits = 0
    for i in range(k):
        if mask >> i & 1:
            lcm = lcm // gcd(lcm, d[i]) * d[i]
            bits += 1
    # N // lcm = how many numbers are divisible by all chosen divisors
    cnt = N // lcm
    # Odd-sized subsets are added, even-sized ones subtracted
    if bits % 2 == 1:
        total += cnt
    else:
        total -= cnt
# Brute-force check
brute = 0
for x in range(1, N + 1):
    if x % 2 == 0 or x % 3 == 0 or x % 5 == 0:
        brute += 1
print("N=" + str(N) + " divisors=2 3 5")
print("inclusion-exclusion count = " + str(total))
print("brute force count = " + str(brute))
# Time O(2^k * k), space O(1); the brute force is O(N * k)

followUps:
With k = 40 there are 240 ≈ 1012 subsets, far too many, so you walk the subsets as a tree and cut off whole branches that cannot contribute.

  1. Remove useless divisors first: duplicates, and any number that is a multiple of another one in the list.
  2. Do a DFS that decides "take or skip" for each divisor and carries the running lcm and the sign.
  3. As soon as the lcm is larger than N, stop: ⌊N/lcm⌋ is 0 for this subset and for everything built on it.
void go(int i, long lcm, int sign) {
  if (lcm > N) return;                 // prune
  if (i == k) { total += sign * (N / lcm); return; }
  go(i + 1, lcm, sign);
  go(i + 1, lcm / gcd(lcm, d[i]) * d[i], -sign);
}

Start with go(0, 1, −1) and add N at the end to cancel the empty-set term. For N = 100 the subset {2, 3, 5, 7} already has lcm 210 and is cut. The lcm at least doubles per element, so only subsets of about log2 N elements survive.

The Möbius function μ(d) is the inclusion–exclusion sign stored once per number: μ(d) = +1 or −1 when d is a product of an even or odd number of different primes, and 0 when d contains a squared prime.

So a loop over subsets of primes becomes a loop over divisors. The count of numbers in 1..N coprime with n is sum over d dividing n of μ(d)·⌊N/d⌋. Divisors with a repeated prime drop out because those are not real subsets.

Example n = 6, N = 10: divisors 1, 2, 3, 6 have μ = +1, −1, −1, +1, giving 10 − 5 − 3 + 1 = 3, which are 1, 5 and 7. All μ values up to N come from a sieve in O(N log log N), or O(N) with a linear sieve. The same idea counts coprime pairs: sum of μ(d)·⌊N/d⌋².

code.title: Catalan numbers: the split recurrence checked against C(2n, n)/(n+1)
code.python:
n = 10
cat = [0] * (n + 1)
cat[0] = 1  # one empty object
# First-return split: inner part of size j, outer part of size i-1-j
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    for j in range(i):
        cat[i] += cat[j] * cat[i - 1 - j]
print("Catalan by recurrence: " + " ".join(str(v) for v in cat))

# Closed form: C(2n, n) / (n + 1)
binom = 1
for i in range(n):
    # multiply first, then divide: the division is always exact
    binom = binom * (2 * n - i) // (i + 1)
print("Catalan by formula for n=" + str(n) + ": " + str(binom // (n + 1)))
# Recurrence: O(n^2) time, O(n) space. Formula: O(n) time, O(1) space

followUps:
Use C_n = (2n)! / (n! · (n+1)!) with factorials taken mod p and the two divisions done as modular inverses.

  1. Build fact[0..2n] mod p in one loop.
  2. Find the inverses of fact[n] and fact[n+1] with fast power (exponent p − 2).
  3. Multiply the three numbers.
fact[0] = 1;
for (int i = 1; i <= 2 * n; i++) fact[i] = fact[i-1] * i % p;
long ans = fact[2*n] * power(fact[n], p - 2) % p
                     * power(fact[n+1], p - 2) % p;

Check with n = 3: 720 / (6 · 24) = 5. For n = 106 this is 2·106 multiplications plus two fast powers: O(n + log p) time, O(n) space. It requires p prime and p > 2n, which holds for 109+7. The O(n²) recurrence would need 1012 steps.

Motzkin numbers count the same kind of object as Catalan but with one extra allowed step that does nothing: a path may go up, go down, or stay flat, and still must never dip below the start line.

In the handshake picture: Catalan needs all 2n people to shake hands without crossing arms; Motzkin has n people and some may sit out. The sequences are Catalan 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42 and Motzkin 1, 1, 2, 4, 9, 21.

The recurrence gains one term for "the first step is flat": M(n) = M(n−1) + sum of M(i)·M(n−2−i) for i = 0..n−2. Check: M(3) = M(2) + M(0)·M(1) + M(1)·M(0) = 2 + 1 + 1 = 4. If a counting problem shows 1, 2, 4, 9, 21 rather than 1, 2, 5, 14, look for an optional "skip" move. The DP costs O(n²) time and O(n) space.

code.title: C(n, r) mod m three ways: Pascal's triangle, Lucas, and the parity trick
code.python:
# Pascal's triangle mod m: works for ANY modulus, no division needed
def pascal(n, m):
    c = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
    for i in range(n + 1):
        c[i][0] = 1 % m
        for j in range(1, i + 1):
            c[i][j] = (c[i - 1][j - 1] + c[i - 1][j]) % m
    return c


# Lucas: split n and r into base-p digits and multiply the small binomials
def lucas(n, r, p):
    small = pascal(p - 1, p)
    res = 1
    while n > 0 or r > 0:
        nd, rd = n % p, r % p
        if rd > nd:
            return 0  # a digit of r above the digit of n gives 0
        res = res * small[nd][rd] % p
        n //= p
        r //= p
    return res


# Small n, composite modulus: Pascal, O(n^2) time and space
print("Pascal: C(30,15) mod 1000 = " + str(pascal(30, 1000)[30][15]))
# Huge n, small prime modulus: Lucas, O(p^2 + log n) time
print("Lucas: C(1000000000000,123456789) mod 7 = "
      + str(lucas(1000000000000, 123456789, 7)))
# Only parity needed: C(n, r) is odd exactly when (n & r) == r, O(1)
n, r = 10, 3
print("Parity: C(10,3) is " + ("odd" if (n & r) == r else "even"))

followUps:
Because once n ≥ p the product n! contains p itself as a factor, so fact[n] is 0 mod p, and 0 has no inverse: the formula turns into 0 times something meaningless.

The real binomial is often not 0, because the factors of p in the numerator and the denominator cancel before the remainder is taken. Example p = 5: C(6, 1) = 6, which is 1 mod 5. But fact[6] = 720 ≡ 0, so the factorial method prints 0.

The fix is Lucas' theorem, which only ever uses values below p. Write both numbers in base 5: 6 = (1, 1) and 1 = (0, 1). Then C(6, 1) ≡ C(1, 0)·C(1, 1) = 1, which is correct. The table of factorials is O(p) and each query is O(logp n).

Kummer's theorem says: the number of times a prime p divides C(n, r) equals the number of carries when you add r and n − r in base p.

Example C(10, 3) = 120 = 2³·15, so the answer for p = 2 should be 3. Add 3 and 7 in binary: 011 + 111. Rightmost column 1 + 1 gives a carry; next 1 + 1 + 1 gives a carry; next 0 + 1 + 1 gives a carry. Three carries, as expected.

Useful consequences: C(n, r) is not divisible by p exactly when the addition has no carries, which for p = 2 is the test (n & r) == r; and C(n, r) mod p is 0 as soon as some base-p digit of r is larger than the same digit of n, the zero case in Lucas. Counting the carries takes O(logp n) time.

code.title: Linearity of expectation: average fixed points of a permutation is always 1
code.python:
perms = 0
fixed_total = 0


# Build every permutation of 0..n-1 and count positions where perm[i] == i
def build(pos, n, perm, used):
    global perms, fixed_total
    if pos == n:
        perms += 1
        for i in range(n):
            if perm[i] == i:
                fixed_total += 1
        return
    for v in range(n):
        if used[v]:
            continue
        used[v] = True
        perm[pos] = v
        build(pos + 1, n, perm, used)
        used[v] = False  # undo the choice (backtrack)


# Theory: each position is fixed with chance 1/n, so E = n * (1/n) = 1
for n in range(1, 7):
    perms = 0
    fixed_total = 0
    build(0, n, [0] * n, [False] * n)
    print("n=" + str(n) + ": permutations=" + str(perms)
          + " fixed points in total=" + str(fixed_total)
          + " average=" + str(fixed_total // perms))
# Brute force costs O(n! * n) time; the formula answers in O(1)

followUps:
14.7 rolls on average, which is 6·(1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + 1/5 + 1/6).

Split the wait into six stages, "rolls until the next new face". When k faces have been seen, a roll shows a new one with chance (6 − k)/6, so that stage takes 6/(6 − k) rolls on average. Linearity lets you add the stages even though you never work out how they interact:

6/6 + 6/5 + 6/4 + 6/3 + 6/2 + 6/1 = 1 + 1.2 + 1.5 + 2 + 3 + 6 = 14.7.

The first face is free (1 roll); the last one is the slow part (6 rolls). For n faces the answer is n·Hn, about n·ln n, the coupon collector result. Computing it is one loop: O(n) time, O(1) space.

Write the expected value as a fraction P/Q and print P · Qp−2 mod p, so the division becomes a multiplication by the modular inverse of Q.

long inv = power(Q % p, p - 2);   // fast power mod p
long ans = (P % p) * inv % p;

You do not need to reduce the fraction first: 2/4 and 1/2 give the same residue. In a DP you rarely form P and Q at all; every division by k in the recurrence is replaced on the spot by multiplying with inv(k).

Small check with p = 7: the value 1/2 is 1·inv(2) = 4, because 2·4 = 8 ≡ 1. The dice answer 14.7 = 147/10 is printed as 147·inv(10) mod p. Q must not be a multiple of p. Cost O(log p) per inverse.

code.title: Expected-value DP with a self-loop, in exact fractions
code.python:
from math import gcd

# Game: s squares from the goal, roll a fair 3-sided die (1..3).
# A roll that overshoots is wasted: you stay where you are (self-loop).
S, faces = 6, 3
num = [0] * (S + 1)
den = [1] * (S + 1)  # E[0] = 0/1: already at the goal
print("die faces=" + str(faces) + ", overshoot = stay put")
for s in range(1, S + 1):
    # E[s] = 1 + (1/3) * sum of next states, where bad rolls give E[s] again.
    # Move the E[s] terms left: E[s] = (3 + sum of E[s-d] for valid d) / valid
    sn, sd = faces, 1
    valid = 0
    for d in range(1, min(faces, s) + 1):
        sn = sn * den[s - d] + num[s - d] * sd  # add the fraction E[s-d]
        sd = sd * den[s - d]
        valid += 1
    sd *= valid
    g = gcd(sn, sd)  # keep the fraction reduced
    num[s] = sn // g
    den[s] = sd // g
    print("E[" + str(s) + "] = " + str(num[s]) + "/" + str(den[s]))
# Time O(S * faces), space O(S)

followUps:
42 rolls on average. Use two states: E0 = expected rolls when the last roll was not a six, E1 = expected rolls when the last roll was a six.

  • E0 = 1 + (1/6)·E1 + (5/6)·E0. E0 appears on both sides (a self-loop).
  • E1 = 1 + (1/6)·0 + (5/6)·E0. A second six ends the game; anything else throws you back.

Move the self-loop left in the first line: (1/6)·E0 = 1 + (1/6)·E1, so E0 = 6 + E1. Put that into the second: E1 = 1 + (5/6)(6 + E1) = 6 + (5/6)·E1, so E1 = 36 and E0 = 42.

Sanity check: one six takes 6 rolls, and two in a row takes 6 + 36. The general pattern for a run of length k is 6 + 6² + … + 6k.

They become a problem when the answer must be exact, or when the calculation divides by something tiny, or runs through very many states.

  • Exact output: "print P·Q−1 mod p" cannot be recovered from a double at all; work mod p from the start.
  • 1 − q with q near 1: if a state returns to itself with probability 0.9999999999999999, then 1 − q is about 10−16 and has almost no correct digits, yet you divide by it.
  • Underflow: 0.52000 is stored as exactly 0, so later ratios turn into 0/0. Keep logarithms.
  • Long chains: 106 states each adding an error of 10−16 can still pass a 10−6 tolerance, but subtracting two large nearly equal values will not.

Use double, never float; rearrange to avoid subtractions; compare with a tolerance, not ==.

code.title: Sprague-Grundy: mex table for moves {1,3,4}, XOR across piles
code.python:
moves = [1, 3, 4]
piles = [5, 7, 9]
mx = 9
g = [0] * (mx + 1)  # g[0] = 0: no move, a losing position
for x in range(1, mx + 1):
    # Mark the Grundy numbers of every position reachable from x
    seen = [False] * (len(moves) + 2)
    for s in moves:
        if s <= x:
            seen[g[x - s]] = True
    # mex = smallest non-negative number that is not reachable
    m = 0
    while seen[m]:
        m += 1
    g[x] = m
# Independent piles combine with XOR
xr = 0
for p in piles:
    xr ^= g[p]
print("moves=1 3 4 piles=5 7 9")
print("grundy 0.." + str(mx) + " = " + " ".join(str(v) for v in g))
print("xor of pile grundy numbers = " + str(xr))
print("First player wins" if xr != 0 else "Second player wins")
# Time O(max * |moves| + piles), space O(max)

followUps:
Because two identical games played side by side must cancel out, and XOR is the combination where x with x gives 0, while ordinary addition gives 2x.

With two equal copies, the second player just copies every move in the other copy and so always has a reply; the pair is a loss for whoever moves first, so its value has to be 0. XOR does that; a sum does not.

More exactly, a game with Grundy number g behaves like a single Nim heap of size g, and Nim positions are lost exactly when the XOR of the heaps is 0. Example: components with Grundy numbers 1, 2 and 3. The sum 6 would suggest a win, but 1 XOR 2 XOR 3 = 0, and indeed every move can be answered by restoring XOR 0, so the first player loses.

Because Stone Game is decided by who collects more points, not by who makes the last move, and Sprague–Grundy only covers games where a player with no move loses.

Two further mismatches: the result depends on the scores collected so far, which a Grundy number does not record, and the row of stones is a single component that never splits into independent games, so there is nothing to XOR.

The right tool is interval DP on the score difference: dp[i][j] = max(a[i] − dp[i+1][j], a[j] − dp[i][j−1]), the best lead the player to move can get from stones i..j.

Example [5, 3, 4, 5]: dp for [5,3,4] and [3,4,5] is 4 each, so the full row gives max(5 − 4, 5 − 4) = 1 and the first player wins by 1. Time O(n²), space O(n²), or O(n) with a rolling row.

code.title: Nim: XOR of the heaps decides the winner and gives the winning move
code.python:
def report(heaps):
    # XOR all heap sizes together
    x = 0
    for h in heaps:
        x ^= h
    print("heaps = " + " ".join(str(h) for h in heaps) + ", xor = " + str(x))
    if x == 0:
        # Every move changes one heap, so the XOR must become non-zero
        print("  xor is 0: the first player loses")
        return
    for i in range(len(heaps)):
        # A heap that has the top bit of x gets smaller when XORed with x
        target = heaps[i] ^ x
        if target < heaps[i]:
            print("  first player wins: reduce heap " + str(i)
                  + " from " + str(heaps[i]) + " to " + str(target))
            heaps[i] = target
            break
    check = 0
    for h in heaps:
        check ^= h
    print("  xor after the move = " + str(check))


report([3, 4, 5])
report([1, 2, 3])
# Time O(n), space O(1)

followUps:
In misère Nim (the player who takes the last stone loses) you play exactly like normal Nim until your move would leave only heaps of size 1; at that moment you leave an odd number of them instead of an even number.

The rule in two cases:

  • At least one heap has 2 or more stones: the first player wins exactly when the XOR is not 0, the same as normal Nim.
  • Every heap has 1 stone: the first player wins exactly when the number of heaps is even.

Examples: [1, 1, 1] is a loss, since the players alternate and the first one takes the third stone. [2, 1] has XOR 3, a win: take the whole heap of 2, leaving [1], and the opponent is forced to take the last stone. The check is still O(n) time and O(1) space.

XOR all heaps to get X, then find any heap h where h XOR X is smaller than h, and reduce that heap to h XOR X. One pass, O(n) time and O(1) space.

int X = 0;
for (int h : heaps) X ^= h;
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    if ((heaps[i] ^ X) < heaps[i]) {   // has the top bit of X
        take = heaps[i] - (heaps[i] ^ X);  break;
    }

Such a heap always exists when X is not 0: some heap has the highest set bit of X, and XOR with X switches that bit off, which makes the number smaller whatever happens to the lower bits.

Example [3, 4, 5]: X = 3 XOR 4 XOR 5 = 2. Heap 3 gives 3 XOR 2 = 1, which is smaller than 3, so take 2 stones from it. The new position [1, 4, 5] has XOR 0.
